title: Thella Kaagitham
dek: A sincere youthful drama with something meaningful to say, even when its storytelling feels a generation behind the teenagers it portrays.
review: Thella Kaagitham works best when it looks beyond teenage romance and asks a more useful question: who do young people listen to when emotion becomes stronger than judgment?

The film gives real weight to parents, friends and outside influences. A good friend is not simply someone who supports every decision; sometimes friendship means warning someone, questioning an impulsive choice and helping them see consequences they cannot see in the moment. The film's argument that teenagers should be able to speak openly with their parents also has value.

My larger issue is the way the film presents today's teenagers. At times the setting and behaviour seem deliberately pulled backwards to preserve an older kind of innocence. That creates nostalgia, but today's teenagers have far more exposure to information about relationships, consequences and social behaviour. A contemporary film needs to understand not only that young people make mistakes, but why they make them now.

The second half repeats ideas the audience has already understood. Harsh Roshan is sincere, but the role needs more ease and emotional range. Nakshatra makes a confident impression, while Ajay gives the parental side of the story needed weight. The music supports the film, but did not reach the level I expected from Vijay Bulganin.

Director Ramesh Bandreddy appears sincere about the message. The film is not cynical and it does not treat its subject merely as shock value. A tighter, more contemporary screenplay could have made the same ideas far more powerful.

I liked Thella Kaagitham more than some of the criticism around it suggests. It is imperfect, but it has something meaningful to say about parents listening, children trusting, responsible friendship and the way vulnerable emotions can be manipulated. Could it have been better? Definitely. Is it a bad film? I don't think so.
works: Its sincerity, the friendship angle, parent-child communication, Nakshatra's confident presence and a meaningful core idea.
misses: A dated view of modern teenagers, repetitive second-half writing, uneven pacing and a lead performance that needs more emotional range.
